title: Model Monitoring and Maintenance
summary: A deployed model is not done - the world changes, and model performance drifts as incoming data diverges from training data. Monitoring tracks prediction quality, input distributions, and system health, alerting you when things degrade. Detecting dat
content:
# Model Monitoring and Maintenance ##### The credit model that quietly stopped working A lender deployed a credit-risk model in early 2020. Validation accuracy was 0.89, the API was fast and reliable, uptime was 99.97%, and every dashboard was green. By mid-2020 the model was approving loans it should have declined. Employment history — its strongest feature — had become nearly meaningless when a third of applicants had been furloughed. Income stability signals inverted. The model kept producing confident scores based on a world that no longer existed. **Nothing broke.** No errors, no latency spike, no failed health check. Traditional monitoring showed a perfectly healthy service. The failure was invisible to every metric being collected, because nobody was measuring whether the *predictions* were still any good. This is the defining property of ML systems: **they degrade silently while appearing to work.** Standard observability tells you the service is up; ML monitoring tells you whether it is right. ##### Why models degrade Four causes, and distinguishing them determines the fix. **Data drift** — the input distribution changes while the input-output relationship holds. Your customer base shifts younger; a new region launches; a sensor is recalibrated. The model's logic is still correct, but it is now extrapolating beyond what it saw in training. **Concept drift** — the relationship itself changes. What predicted default in 2019 stopped predicting it in 2020. Even with identical inputs, the correct output is different. Gama et al. (2014) survey this thoroughly; the practical point is that no amount of input monitoring detects it, because the inputs may look entirely normal. **Upstream data changes** — a pipeline modification changes a unit from rupees to lakhs, a column is renamed, a join starts producing nulls. Common, and usually the fastest to fix once detected. **Feedback loops** — the model's own predictions change the world it observes. A recommender that promotes popular items makes them more popular, and future training data reflects the model's influence rather than genuine preference. ##### Data drift versus concept drift This is the assignment's question, and precision matters because the responses differ entirely. | | Data drift | Concept drift | |---|---|---| | What changes | P(X) — the input distribution | P(y\|X) — the relationship | | Example | Average customer age drops from 42 to 29 | Fraud tactics change; old signals stop working | | Detectable from | **Inputs alone** — immediately | **Requires labels** — often delayed | | Model logic | Still valid, but extrapolating | **Now wrong** | | Typical response | Retrain on recent data | Retrain, and reconsider the features | The critical operational asymmetry: **data drift is detectable in real time from inputs; concept drift usually requires ground truth you do not have yet.** A loan default is only known months later. A fraud chargeback arrives weeks after the transaction. That delay is why input monitoring matters so much. It gives you an early warning signal when the true performance signal is unavailable — and in the credit example, the input distribution shifted visibly in March while the default labels confirming it would not arrive until August. ##### Detecting data drift Compare the current input distribution against a stored **reference** — usually the training set. ```python import numpy as np from scipy import stats def detect_numeric_drift(reference: np.ndarray, current: np.ndarray, alpha: float = 0.01) -> dict: """Kolmogorov-Smirnov test plus effect size.""" ks_stat, p_value = stats.ks_2samp(reference, current) # Effect size matters — with large samples, tiny shifts are "significant" pooled_std = np.sqrt((reference.std()**2 + current.std()**2) / 2) effect = abs(current.mean() - reference.mean()) / (pooled_std + 1e-9) return { "ks_statistic": round(float(ks_stat), 4), "p_value": float(p_value), "effect_size": round(float(effect), 3), "drifted": bool(p_value < alpha and effect > 0.2), # BOTH conditions "ref_mean": round(float(reference.mean()), 3), "cur_mean": round(float(current.mean()), 3), } ``` Requiring **both** statistical significance and a meaningful effect size is important. With 100,000 samples, a KS test flags a mean shift of 0.3% as significant — technically true and operationally irrelevant. Alert fatigue from over-sensitive drift detection is a real failure mode, and the effect-size condition prevents it. For categorical features, **Population Stability Index** is the standard, and it comes with widely-used thresholds: ```python def population_stability_index(reference, current, bins=10) -> float: """PSI: <0.1 stable, 0.1-0.25 moderate shift, >0.25 significant.""" edges = np.histogram_bin_edges(reference, bins=bins) ref_pct = np.histogram(reference, bins=edges)[0] / len(reference) cur_pct = np.histogram(current, bins=edges)[0] / len(current) eps = 1e-6 # avoid division by zero ref_pct, cur_pct = ref_pct + eps, cur_pct + eps return float(np.sum((cur_pct - ref_pct) * np.log(cur_pct / ref_pct))) ``` Beyond individual features, monitor **prediction drift** — the distribution of model outputs. It is a single number that catches many problems at once, including feature interactions that per-feature tests miss: ```python def check_prediction_drift(ref_probs, current_probs) -> dict: return { "psi": population_stability_index(ref_probs, current_probs), "ref_positive_rate": float((ref_probs > 0.5).mean()), "cur_positive_rate": float((current_probs > 0.5).mean()), "mean_shift": float(current_probs.mean() - ref_probs.mean()), } ``` If your fraud model's positive rate jumps from 2% to 9% overnight, something is wrong — either the world changed dramatically or, far more likely, an upstream pipeline broke. **Evidently** packages all of this with reports and dashboards: ```python from evidently.report import Report from evidently.metric_preset import DataDriftPreset, TargetDriftPreset report = Report(metrics=[DataDriftPreset(), TargetDriftPreset()]) report.run(reference_data=reference_df, current_data=current_df) report.save_html("drift_report.html") result = report.as_dict() n_drifted = result["metrics"][0]["result"]["number_of_drifted_columns"] ``` ##### Logging predictions You cannot monitor what you did not record. Every prediction should be logged with enough context to reconstruct it later. ```python from datetime import datetime, timezone import uuid, json async def log_prediction(features: dict, probability: float, model_version: str, latency_ms: float) -> str: prediction_id = str(uuid.uuid4()) await db.execute( """INSERT INTO predictions (prediction_id, ts, model_version, features, probability, predicted_class, latency_ms) VALUES ($1, $2, $3, $4, $5, $6, $7)""", prediction_id, datetime.now(timezone.utc), model_version, json.dumps(features), probability, int(probability >= 0.5), latency_ms, ) return prediction_id ``` The **`prediction_id` returned to the caller** is what makes the feedback loop possible. When the outcome becomes known — the loan defaults, the transaction is charged back — the caller reports it against that ID: ```sql CREATE TABLE prediction_outcomes ( prediction_id UUID PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES predictions(prediction_id), actual_label SMALLINT NOT NULL, observed_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(), source TEXT NOT NULL -- 'chargeback', 'manual_review', 'default' ); ``` Once you have that table, **true performance monitoring** becomes a query rather than a project: ```sql SELECT date_trunc('week', p.ts) AS week, p.model_version, COUNT(*) AS n, ROUND(AVG(p.probability)::numeric, 4) AS avg_score, ROUND(AVG(o.actual_label)::numeric, 4) AS actual_rate, ROUND(AVG((p.predicted_class = o.actual_label)::int)::numeric, 4) AS accuracy FROM predictions p JOIN prediction_outcomes o USING (prediction_id) WHERE p.ts >= now() - interval '12 weeks' GROUP BY week, p.model_version ORDER BY week DESC; ``` That query, run weekly, is what the lender lacked. The accuracy column would have fallen visibly month by month. ##### What to monitor, and alerting Four layers, each answering a different question: | Layer | Metrics | Answers | |---|---|---| | **Infrastructure** | Latency p50/p95, error rate, throughput, memory | Is the service healthy? | | **Data** | Feature drift, null rate, range violations, schema | Are the inputs as expected? | | **Model** | Prediction distribution, confidence, positive rate | Is behaviour changing? | | **Business** | Accuracy on labelled outcomes, precision, revenue impact | Is it still *right*? | Alerts should fire on symptoms that matter, with thresholds tuned to avoid noise: ```yaml - alert: FeatureDriftDetected expr: model_feature_psi > 0.25 for: 6h # sustained, not a momentary blip labels: {severity: warning} annotations: summary: "Feature {{ $labels.feature }} PSI {{ $value }} (threshold 0.25)" runbook: "https://wiki/runbooks/feature-drift" - alert: PredictionRateAnomaly expr: | abs(rate(model_positive_predictions[1h]) / rate(model_predictions[1h]) - 0.02) > 0.015 for: 2h labels: {severity: critical} - alert: AccuracyBelowThreshold expr: model_rolling_accuracy_7d < 0.80 for: 1h labels: {severity: critical} - alert: NoPredictionsReceived # the silent-failure detector expr: rate(model_predictions_total[30m]) == 0 for: 30m labels: {severity: critical} ``` That last alert catches what none of the others can: an integration that stopped calling your model entirely. A model receiving zero traffic looks perfectly healthy by every other metric. ##### Retraining strategies Four approaches, and the choice depends on how fast your domain moves: **Scheduled** — retrain weekly or monthly regardless. Simple and predictable; wasteful when nothing changed and too slow when something did. **Triggered** — retrain when drift or accuracy degradation crosses a threshold. Efficient, and requires monitoring you trust. **Continuous** — retrain on a rolling window constantly. Appropriate for fast-moving domains like ad click prediction; operationally demanding. **Manual** — a human decides. Correct for high-stakes models where an automated retrain on bad data is unacceptable. ```python def should_retrain(metrics: dict) -> tuple[bool, str]: """Explicit, auditable retraining policy.""" if metrics["rolling_accuracy_7d"] < 0.80: return True, "accuracy below floor" if metrics["max_feature_psi"] > 0.25: return True, "significant feature drift" if metrics["days_since_training"] > 90: return True, "scheduled refresh" if metrics["new_category_rate"] > 0.05: return True, "unseen categories in inputs" return False, "within tolerance" ``` The rule that prevents disasters: **automated retraining must never auto-deploy.** The pipeline trains, evaluates against thresholds, compares to the current champion, and registers a candidate — then a human promotes it. A pipeline that deploys automatically will eventually train on corrupted data and ship it, and by then the previous model is gone from serving. Deploy retrained models through **shadow mode** first — running alongside the incumbent on live traffic with predictions logged but unused — then canary at 5%, then full. The shadow phase catches problems with zero risk. ```mermaid flowchart TD A[Predictions served] --> B[Log features + output
+ prediction_id] B --> C[(Prediction store)] D[Outcomes arrive
days to months later] --> E[Join on prediction_id] C --> E C --> F[Input drift checks
KS, PSI — real time] E --> G[True accuracy
— delayed] F --> H{Drift detected?} G --> I{Accuracy dropped?} H -->|yes| J[Alert + investigate] I -->|yes| J J --> K{Upstream bug or
genuine drift?} K -->|bug| L[Fix pipeline — do NOT retrain] K -->|drift| M[Retrain on recent data] M --> N[Evaluate vs champion] N --> O[Shadow → canary → full] ``` That branch at the bottom matters. **Investigate before retraining.** If a feature's distribution shifted because an upstream job started sending values in different units, retraining teaches the model to accept corrupted data — you have automated the propagation of a bug. ##### Common mistakes - **Monitoring only infrastructure** — the credit model's dashboards were all green. - **No prediction logging**, so drift analysis is impossible retrospectively. - **No `prediction_id`** linking predictions to eventual outcomes. - **Statistical significance without effect size**, producing alert fatigue. - **Retraining without investigating** the cause, propagating upstream bugs. - **Automated retraining that auto-deploys.** - **No baseline stored** at deployment time to compare against. - **Ignoring delayed labels**, so true performance is never measured. - **Retraining on drifted data** that includes the bad period. - **No "zero predictions" alert**, missing complete integration failures. ##### Your hands-on tie-in The practical task: **add logging and a simple drift check to a deployed model**, then simulate drifted input and detect the change. Generate the drift deliberately — shift one feature's mean by two standard deviations — and confirm your PSI or KS test fires. A detector you have never seen trigger is a detector you should not rely on. The mini project is a **monitoring dashboard** tracking prediction distributions with drift alerts. Include all four layers: latency and error rate, per-feature drift, prediction distribution, and — where you have labels — rolling accuracy. Evidently generates the drift reports; Grafana or Streamlit can display them. Add the "no predictions in 30 minutes" alert, because it is three lines and catches the failure the others cannot see. For the assignment, **explain data drift versus concept drift with an example of each, and how you would respond**. Be precise about the distinction — P(X) changing versus P(y|X) changing — and about the operational consequence: data drift is detectable immediately from inputs, while concept drift requires ground truth that often arrives months later. For responses, cover the investigate-first rule: confirm whether the shift is a genuine world change or an upstream data bug, because retraining on a bug bakes it in. The 2020 credit model is a clean illustration of both drifting simultaneously. ##### Key takeaways - ML systems degrade silently — infrastructure monitoring shows a healthy service while predictions become worthless. - Data drift changes the input distribution and is detectable immediately; concept drift changes the input-output relationship and usually needs delayed labels to confirm. - Log every prediction with features, output and a `prediction_id`, so outcomes can be joined later to measure true accuracy. - Require both statistical significance and meaningful effect size before alerting, and always include a zero-traffic alert. - Investigate before retraining — an upstream data bug looks exactly like drift, and retraining on it automates the corruption.
